lede: Water moves on its own, through the membrane around every cell, from where there is more of it to where there is less. That one movement decides whether a plant stands up or wilts, and it is the whole of Prescribed Practical B5.
can: Define osmosis in the specification's words and say which way water moves in any situation.
Name a cell as turgid, flaccid or plasmolysed, and describe what its membrane has done.
Work out a percentage change in mass and read the point of no change off a graph.

md: Stand a limp stick of celery in water overnight and it comes out crisp. Leave the same stick on the worktop and it goes floppy. One kind of cell, two opposite endings — and the only thing that moved was water.

text: 1. Water goes where there is less of it

md:
A **selectively permeable** membrane has pores that let small molecules through and hold large ones back. Water is small, so it crosses freely. Sugar is too big, so it stays put.

The dilute side holds **more water per cubic centimetre**, so more water molecules reach the membrane from that side each second. Overall, water flows towards the concentrated solution.

prompt: Across a selectively permeable membrane, water moves out of the dilute solution and into the more ______ one.
explain: Concentrated. Water moves to where there is less of it — that is the whole idea in six words.

md:
**A is turgid.** Water has come in, the vacuole is full, and it pushes the cytoplasm and the cell membrane hard against the cell wall. A plant full of turgid cells stands up.
**B is flaccid.** Water has gone out, the vacuole has shrunk, and the membrane no longer presses on the wall. The plant droops.
**C is plasmolysed.** So much water has left that the **cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall**.

prompt: Which cell has been sitting in the most concentrated solution?
explain: C. The more concentrated the solution outside, the more water leaves — and C has lost the most.

text: 3. What a plasmolysed cell really looks like

alt: Light micrograph of red onion epidermis cells after being mounted in a concentrated solution: each cell keeps a straight-sided rigid wall, while the red-purple contents have shrunk into a rounded blob that has separated from the wall, leaving a clear gap.
credit: Trương Minh Khải, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
caption: Red onion cells in a strong solution. The straight lines are the walls; the coloured blobs are the contents, pulled in.
prompt: The examiner shows you this and asks what has happened to the cell membrane. What is the one sentence that earns the mark — and why is 'the cell wall has pulled away' not it?

md: Look at the outlines. Every cell still has **straight sides**, because the wall is rigid cellulose and has not moved at all. What has moved is everything inside it.

prompt: In the photograph, which structure has moved?
options: the cell membrane, away from the wall
the cell wall, away from the membrane
answer: the cell membrane, away from the wall
explain: The membrane. Keep the two nouns in that order and the mark is yours.

text: 4. A worked answer, start to finish

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Osmosis"
why: Five minutes on the same three cell states, worth watching now that you have met them.

title: Worked example: 'Name state C and explain how the cell reached it. [3]'
md:
**Step 1 — name it.** C is plasmolysed. One word, and 'shrunk' is not it.
**Step 2 — say what moved.** The cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall.
**Step 3 — give the cause.** The solution outside was more concentrated than the cell sap, so water left the vacuole and cytoplasm by osmosis and the contents shrank.

Each step is one mark, and they go in that order because each one explains the next.

prompt: Finish step 3 in your own words: water left the cell because the solution outside was more ______ than the cell sap.
explain: Concentrated. Naming which side is more concentrated is what turns a definition into an answer about this cell.

md:
Put a plant cell in pure water and water floods in — but the **cell wall limits the entry of water**. Once the cell is turgid the wall will not stretch any further, so no more water can get in.

An **animal cell** has no wall. Water keeps entering until the membrane splits and the cell bursts. In a concentrated solution the same animal cell loses water and shrivels instead.

prompt: A plant cell in pure water does not burst because the cell ______ limits the entry of water.
explain: Wall. It is the single word that separates the plant cell's ending from the animal cell's.

md:
Cut cylinders of carrot to the same length, blot them, weigh them, and leave one in each sucrose solution for a day. Blot and reweigh. Then work out, for each one:

**percentage change = change in mass ÷ mass at the start × 100**

The divisor is the mass you **started** with, every time.

prompt: A cylinder weighs 4.20 g at the start and 4.83 g after 24 hours in pure water. What is its percentage change in mass? Give the number only.
explain: 4.83 − 4.20 = +0.63 g, and +0.63 ÷ 4.20 × 100 = +15.0%. Dividing by 4.83 would have lost the mark.

md: Visking tubing has the same trick as a cell membrane: small pores, water through, sugar not. Water moves **into** the bag, the volume inside rises, and the level in the capillary tube climbs. The one thing never to say is that the **sugar** moved — it cannot fit.

task: Put a different number of particles on each side of the membrane and watch which way the net movement goes. Then say in one sentence why a carrot cylinder in pure water gains mass, using the words dilute, concentrated and selectively permeable.

prompt: The level in the Visking tubing's capillary rises. Why?
options: Water moved into the tubing, so the volume inside increased
Sugar moved out of the tubing into the beaker
The tubing absorbed sugar from the water
answer: Water moved into the tubing, so the volume inside increased
explain: Only the water can cross. More water inside means more liquid inside, so the level rises.

title: You can now…

md:
Say which solution is the more concentrated, and which way water moves.
Name the partially permeable membrane in the answer.
Explain what happens to a plant cell, and to an animal cell.
Work out a percentage change and use it.

Six to eight marks, usually a whole question with a diagram, a calculation and an explanation; the same content is Prescribed Practical B5. Four sentences answer it: name the two solutions and say which is the stronger, give the direction of the water, name the membrane, then finish on whatever was asked — the level, the mass, the length or the cells.
